question: According to a Le Figaro report1 dated 17 July 2026, on 11 May 2026 a Frontex aircraft filmed the transfer of 90 people from a fast boat equipped with two 300-PS engines to the Sea-Watch 5’s rubber dinghies, approximately 45 nautical miles north-east of Tripoli.

It further stated that the boat was being operated by five masked men in paramilitary uniforms, who distributed life jackets to the migrants, coordinated the transfer and then sped off towards the Libyan coast.

The video footage has been submitted to the Brindisi Public Prosecutor’s Office, and the captain of the Sea-Watch 5, Anne van Dam, is thus under investigation on suspicion of aiding and abetting illegal immigration under aggravating circumstances.

The case raises questions as to the oversight of private sea-rescue organisations in the Mediterranean, any EU funding they may receive and the role of Frontex intelligence material in national criminal cases. 1.
Is the Commission aware of the incident of 11 May 2026 and the video footage recorded by Frontex, and has it been informed of it by Frontex or by the Italian authorities?

In view of the repeatedly documented pattern of such incidents, does the Commission intend to propose a binding code of conduct for private sea-rescue organisations in the Mediterranean, for example regarding the sharing of vessel positions or the coordination of operations for the transfer of persons at sea?

Does the Commission believe the existing legal framework under the SAR, SOLAS and Palermo Conventions to be sufficient to distinguish between genuine emergencies at sea and organised people-transfer operations carried out by people-smugglers, or does it see a need for any changes to be made?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (15.9.2026) The Commission is aware of the reports concerning the alleged incident of 11 May 2026 involving the vessel Sea-Watch 5 and related judicial proceedings in Italy. Preventing migrant smuggling while protecting life at sea remains a key priority.

Assistance to persons in distress at sea is an obligation under international law, and suspected criminal conducts must be investigated. Under international maritime law, coordination of search and rescue operations are a responsibility of the competent national authorities.

The international legal framework, including the International Conventions on Maritime Search and Rescue, Safety of Life at Sea and Transnational Organised Crime, together with relevant EU legislation, provides the basis for search and rescue activities and the fight against migrant smuggling.

The Commission has also proposed new rules to improve the investigation and prosecution of smuggling networks and reinforce European Union Agency for Law Enforcement Cooperation’s (Europol) role, and more recently, a new EU sanctions regime to freeze smugglers’ assets, restrict their movements and cut off their profits.

These efforts are complemented by the Global Alliance to Counter Migrant Smuggling, which strengthens cooperation with third countries and international organisations. The Commission continues to work with Member States through the Search and Rescue (SAR) Contact Group1 and engages with other stakeholders carrying out search and rescue operations.
At present, the Commission is not planning to propose a binding EU code of conduct for private vessels.
1 The SAR Contact Group aims at enhancing cooperation and information exchange between Member States, as
well as with other relevant stakeholders, in the field of search and rescue. The last meeting of the SAR Contact Group took place in May 2026.
